{"parentUuid":"67bb3918-28fb-4dbf-9e04-be057f1a68d6","isSidechain":true,"promptId":"e8d5459a-a357-48d8-90fc-44d59227e184","agentId":"af5a83bcca1649bc3","type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01Q7fh4oGSsvKGbDte1xhNRM","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# bench-harness improvement plan\n2\t\n3\t## The thesis\n4\t\n5\tThe harness is good at **refusing** and weak at **volunteering**.\n6\t\n7\tRefusing is what it was built for and it works. Across this campaign it killed five optimization\n8\tcandidates cheaply and correctly, caught an operator contaminating a live measurement, inverted a\n9\tconclusion that a −17.4% number would otherwise have cemented, and corrected a headline result from\n10\tfive wins to three. Twenty-nine of its own defects were found by using it; twenty-five are fixed;\n11\t324 checks are green across eight suites.\n12\t\n13\tVolunteering is where the remaining value is. Almost every insight that redirected this campaign was a\n14\t**synthesis the tool had all the data for and left to the reader**: that the largest deltas were the\n15\tunresolvable ones, that a row had never once been measurable across four attempts, that 70% of a row\n16\tbelongs to code no kernel change can touch, that the top budget candidate was the benchmark's own\n17\tclosure. The operator this tool exists for demonstrably skims. Every item in section A converts\n18\tsomething already in the store into something the report says out loud.\n19\t\n20\tOrdering is by value, not by cost. Section A first.\n21\t\n22\t---\n23\t\n24\t## A. Make the tool volunteer what it already knows\n25\t\n26\t### A1. Flag when the largest movements are the unresolvable ones\n27\t\n28\t**Evidence.** In the replicated sweep the two biggest deltas on the board, −12.5% and −10.7%, were\n29\tboth flat, while a −7.1% row was a win. That inversion is the single most counterintuitive fact the\n30\tcampaign produced and the reader has to notice it unaided by scanning fifteen rows.\n31\t\n32\t**Change.** After the table, when any row in the top three by |delta| is `Flat` or `BelowResolution`,\n33\tsay so explicitly and name the leg count that would change it.\n34\t\n35\t**Acceptance.** Fires on the replicated sweep naming both rows. Silent on a run where the largest\n36\tdeltas resolve. Both directions tested, from the real stored legs.\n37\t\n38\t### A2. Cross-reference a row against its own history in the store\n39\t\n40\t**Evidence.** `emittingClausesPayRegionRebuild` produced −9.78%, then \"unmeasurable\", then −9.5%, then\n41\t−12.5%-flat across four separate attempts. Every one of those is in the store. Across this campaign it killed five optimization\ncandidates cheaply and correctly, caught an operator contaminating a live measurement, inverted a\nconclusion that a −17.4% number would otherwise have cemented, and corrected a headline result from\nfive wins to three. Twenty-nine of its own defects were found by using it; twenty-five are fixed;\n324 checks are green across eight suites.\n\nVolunteering is where the remaining value is. Almost every insight that redirected this campaign was a\n**synthesis the tool had all the data for and left to the reader**: that the largest deltas were the\nunresolvable ones, that a row had never once been measurable across four attempts, that 70% of a row\nbelongs to code no kernel change can touch, that the top budget candidate was the benchmark's own\nclosure. The operator this tool exists for demonstrably skims. Every item in section A converts\nsomething already in the store into something the report says out loud.\n\nOrdering is by value, not by cost. Section A first.\n\n---\n\n## A. Make the tool volunteer what it already knows\n\n### A1. Flag when the largest movements are the unresolvable ones\n\n**Evidence.** In the replicated sweep the two biggest deltas on the board, −12.5% and −10.7%, were\nboth flat, while a −7.1% row was a win. That inversion is the single most counterintuitive fact the\ncampaign produced and the reader has to notice it unaided by scanning fifteen rows.\n\n**Change.** After the table, when any row in the top three by |delta| is `Flat` or `BelowResolution`,\nsay so explicitly and name the leg count that would change it.\n\n**Acceptance.** Fires on the replicated sweep naming both rows. Silent on a run where the largest\ndeltas resolve. Both directions tested, from the real stored legs.\n\n### A2. Cross-reference a row against its own history in the store\n\n**Evidence.** `emittingClausesPayRegionRebuild` produced −9.78%, then \"unmeasurable\", then −9.5%, then\n−12.5%-flat across four separate attempts. Every one of those is in the store. Three times a verdict\nabout that row was recorded and later withdrawn, and nothing ever said \"this row has disagreed with\nitself before\".\n\n**Change.** A comparison consults the store for prior runs on the same rows and flags any row whose\ncurrent verdict contradicts a previous one, or whose deltas across runs exceed its own resolution.\n\n**Acceptance.** On the current store it names `emittingClausesPayRegionRebuild` and does **not** name\n`continuationBodiesFuse`, which has been consistent across every measurement.\n\n**Risk to watch.** This is the most speculative item here: \"contradicts\" needs a definition that does\nnot fire on every ordinary re-measurement. Prefer under-firing.\n\n### A3. Per-row noise share, not one global number\n\n**Evidence.** `noiseShare` exists, computes a whole-run figure, and warns above 25%. Say when a budget candidate is not kernel code\n\n**Evidence.** The top entry in the budget-proximity ranking, above every kernel method, is\n`ProtoKernelBench::run$56` at 379 B refused 10/10. It is the benchmark's own closure. The tool ranks\nit helpfully and never mentions that optimizing it would be optimizing the benchmark.\n\n**Change.** Partition the ranking into kernel and non-kernel by package prefix and label it.\n\n**Acceptance.** `run$56` appears under a non-kernel heading; `dispatch$1` and `Stack::grow` under\nkernel.\n\n### A5. Run `BenchPlan` automatically before a bracket\n\n**Evidence.** `BenchPlan` now reproduces real thresholds exactly, verified against all fifteen rows of\nthe replicated sweep. It still runs only on request. Sessions were spent reporting a 25% regression on\na row that resolves to ±22.6%, and the tool could have said so beforehand from data already stored.\n\n**Change.** A bracket forecasts from any prior legs in its store before measuring, and warns, naming\nrows that cannot resolve the target. Refusing outright is probably too strong; the operator may be\nmeasuring exactly to improve the estimate.\n\n**Acceptance.** A bracket on the current store prints the forecast first. A bracket on an empty store\nsays it has no basis to forecast from, rather than silently skipping.\n\n---\n\n## B. Ergonomics that cost real time\n\n### B1. `bench session <store>`\n\nRe-reading a five-leg bracket currently means assembling ten `--control`/`--variant` flags with a\nshell loop, and getting the arm split right by hand. A store plus a session id already determines\nthis. **Acceptance:** one command reproduces the replicated verdict for a stored bracket.\n\n### B2. Invert the fork default\n\nEvery report in this campaign carries \"-f 1 is diagnostic and not a claim\", and `-f 3` was never once\nrun. The label is doing the work that a default should. **Change:** `-f 3` for anything that renders a\nverdict; `-f 1` behind `--diagnostic`. **Acceptance:** the existing label becomes unreachable without\nthe flag.\n\n### B3. If that file is deleted, the run is exactly\nas unrecoverable as the headline pair was, and nothing notices. **Change:** on load, check referenced\nfiles still exist and mark the run's configuration unverifiable if not. **Acceptance:** deleting\n`forced-inline.cmd` makes the sweep replication report its configuration as unverifiable.\n\n---\n\n## C. That is a deliberate stop against the default, and it is the one place\nin this ledger where I have not taken my own recorded default.\n\nEverything else below is finished work, kept for its reasoning.\n\n## DIS-1 is refuted, by measurement, in three forms\n\nVariant 3 halves the handler regression (+11.2% against +21.7%) and avoids the allocation cliff\n(+24 B/op against +240,000), and delivers **no win**: `continuationBodiesFuse` is flat at -0.7%\nagainst the -6.8% that forcing the whole 607-byte body inline delivers.\n\nThe win comes from inlining the whole body, and a small inlined fast path does not approximate it.\nWhat helps the target row is exactly what breaks `trailingMapsStayLinear`'s escape analysis, and\nshrinking what gets inlined shrinks the win with it. See `bench-results/tier3/RESULT.md`.\n\nOpen: whether some other shape recovers the win without enlarging the compilation unit. Nothing\nmeasured suggests one, and proposing another without a mechanism would be guessing.\n\n## The central question, answered with replication\n\nFirst bracket with a real threshold: A/A null clean, `continuationBodiesFuse` **-6.8%** when\n`dispatch$1` is forced inline. The headline survives.\n\nThe correction is on the other row: `trailingMapsStayLinear`'s **timing** regression is *not*\nestablished. It resolves to ±22.64%, so the +23.8% and +26.6% I reported from single legs were\noutside their legs' resolution rather than measured. Its **allocation** regression is established and\nunaffected: +240,000 B/op, exact, matching two independent earlier measurements.\n\nExposed one defect, fixed: mechanisms are suppressed on flat rows, so a 240,000 B/op change showed\nonly as a column entry. Allocation does not need the timing to resolve. See\n`bench-results/bracket1/RESULT.md`.\n\n## Re-measurement done, and it overturned a correction\n\n`-wi 25` settles `emittingClausesPayRegionRebuild`: its error falls from ±12.33 to ±2.97 and the\nblocker clears, exit 0. The row is a **-9.5% win** after all. So the original hand number was roughly\nright, my intermediate correction (\"never a win, it is flat\") was wrong, and the truth is the leg was\n*unmeasurable*. The tool had said so correctly by refusing the whole comparison; I read the refusal\nas a verdict. See `bench-results/exp6/RESULT.md`.\n\n**Superseded by the replication, which is the fourth reading of this row and the first with a\nthreshold: -12.5%, and flat.** So \"a -9.5% win after all\" does not stand either. Across four attempts\nthis row has produced -9.78%, \"unmeasurable\", -9.5% and -12.5%, and the only claim consistent with all\nfour is that **it has never been measurable**, not that it moves and not that it does not. Its control\nleg is flagged for a warmup ramp in the replication too, the same failure it has shown every time.\n\nThe settling problem moved rather than vanished: `handleLoopFusesContinuation` now reports ±14.55%\nand is flat at -8.8%. One re-measurement does not buy a clean sweep, and the tool is saying so.\n\n## The CLI surface has now been QA'd, and it was the softest part of the tool\n\nEvery earlier defect was found by using the tool on a kernel question. Nobody had ever run its\ncommands *wrong*. Six probes with a typo, a missing file and a mismatched argument count found three\ndefects, one of them the campaign's own failure shape: **a store that does not exist read as a store\nthat is empty**, `no runs stored`, exit 0. A mistyped `--store` was indistinguishable from a store\nwhose runs were gone.\n\nAll three fixed, pinned by six new checks; **193 checks green** across five suites. See defects 14 to\n16 in `tool-defects.md`. One observation about kyo itself came out of it: `KyoAppRunner.onResult`\nprints a failed result and then rethrows it, so every kyo app renders its `Abort` failures twice.\n\n## Phase 5 is done: allocation is attributed to the method that allocated it\n\nThe flat table says `Nested` is 50.7% of this row's allocation and can never say by whom. The\ncollapsed view can, and now does, validated end to end on a real JMH run rather than on a fixture:\n\n    kyo.kernel.proto.Nested                    minted at kyo.kernel.proto.Nested$.apply   (3790 samples, ~1.99 GB)\n    kyo.kernel.bench.ProtoKernelBench$$anon$95 minted at ProtoKernelBench$.ask            (3676 samples, ~1.93 GB)\n\nBoth views come from **one** recording, so the conservation check measures the parse: exact, 7,481\nsamples across 1,951 collapsed lines, nothing lost. Two recordings of the same planted program differ\nby 0.25%, and the gate correctly refuses that pair, which is the whole reason the single-recording\nrequirement is in the plan.\n\nAcceptance is a planted program whose only significant allocator is named before the parser runs, not\nconservation, which holds equally for a correct attribution and for one assigning every sample to an\narbitrary frame.\n\nTwo parser defects found on the way, both the character-class family that has bitten this file four\ntimes: an array type truncated at the bracket (`java.lang.Object[]` and `java.lang.Object` became one\nrow, and on the kernel rows the `Object[]` is the stack), and JVM-internal C++ frames truncated at the\n`::`, one of them reported as a method called `void`.\n\n**220 checks green.**\n\n## Phase 6 Tier A is done: every delta now arrives with its next experiment\n\nA comparison used to say a row moved and stop. It now offers the falsifiers that could contradict the\nobvious reading of it, each one flag and one run: force the refused method, raise only the budget it\nis over, force the *control*'s refused method to test whether the win was the inlining rather than the\ndesign, disable escape analysis when allocation moved. The megamorphism and GC falsifiers are\ndeliberately absent, the first unstatable from a log that profiles a receiver at 12 sites in 5,093,\nthe second impossible while every leg pins heap and collector.\n\nThe gate that makes an answer worth having: **a falsifier whose flag did not take refutes nothing.**\n`CompileCommand=inline` is a hint and HotSpot still refuses on `MaxInlineLevel`, node budget, or a\nmethod it cannot compile, so a pipeline without this gate refutes every hypothesis and passes its own\nacceptance. A confirm additionally requires that *only* the instructed method's verdict moved, since\nforcing a callee spends the caller's remaining budget.\n\nAcceptance runs in both directions, which is what the earlier design got wrong: a planted true\nhypothesis must be **confirmed** and a planted false one **refuted**, so an always-refutes\nimplementation fails half of it. Three further answers are distinguished from both: the flag never\nfired, the row half-moved, and the experiment never had the power to separate the two.\n\n**255 checks green** across seven suites.\n\nRun against the campaign's own sweep, the rule table proposes **exactly the experiment I ran by hand**\nin experiment 4, and adjudicates it from stored data: `trailingMapsStayLinear` rides scalar\nreplacement, CONFIRMED, 2,321,410 to 2,561,410 B/op against a target of 2,561,387. That round trip\nfound three more defects, two of them in the investigator itself and one much worse: adding a field to\n`Run` had made **every stored run undecodable**, all 34 of them. See defects 17 to 19.\n\n## The guards that had never fired, exercised\n\nThree of the harness's own guards had never once been triggered, which is the same shape as the CLI\nthat had never been run wrong. Exercising them found four more defects (20 to 23):\n\n- **A leg could have adopted the previous leg's numbers.** The results json is a fixed path per label\n  and was never deleted; JMH exits 0 when its selector matches nothing, so such a run would parse the\n  previous attempt's file, pass the row-count check, and be stored as a measurement of sources it\n  never ran against. Deleted before every attempt now, and its absence fails the leg.\n- **The red-tree gate does work**, verified by planting a failing test in the throwaway worktree. Its\n  message did not: `Failure(1)` under several hundred lines of *passing* test names.\n- **A QA check asserted nothing** on every run ever made (`isEmpty || contains`).\n- **The compile-time steady-state limit cannot be calibrated from any data this campaign has**, and\n  saying so is the honest result. It was 50 ms against an observed maximum of 9 ms across 52 rows.\n  The plan's proposed 4 ms would fire on 8 of those 52, all ordinary. Bounded at 0.5% and labelled\n  not-yet-validated; `Row.unsettledStart` is the signal actually doing this work.\n\n**260 checks green** across seven suites.\n\n## DIS-2 answered, and the answer is that it was never tested\n\nSecond in the plan's run order because it needs no source change. The tool says\n`continuationBodiesFuse` is **-17.4%** under `-XX:FreqInlineSize=600`, more than twice the -6.8% that\nforcing `dispatch$1` delivered, which invites the conclusion that the budget is the whole story.\n\nThe efficacy gate says the opposite. `dispatch$1` is **607 B and refused for `hot method too big` in\nboth logs**: 600 is below 607, so the flag never reached the method the hypothesis is about, and 700\nwas refused for a different reason in experiment 2. The 37 verdicts that did move are almost entirely\nthe *benchmark's own* closures, `run$57` through `run$67` at 119 B going from 1 inlined site to 3,\nplus two `anon$` constructors and `ask`. Every kernel method checked is unchanged.\n\nSo a JVM flag made the benchmark's harness code inline better and the row got faster because of that.\n**DIS-2 is untested, not confirmed**, and the number its mechanism is worth remains the replicated\n-6.8%. See `bench-results/dis2/RESULT.md`.\n\nOne defect out of it: the compilation log is XML, so a constructor arrived as `&lt;init&gt;` while\nevery other tool in the ladder prints `<init>`, and those names cross-referenced against none of them,\nsilently. **264 checks green.**\n\n## C1 refuted, for the cost of reading a profile already on disk\n\nThird in the run order and the plan's own \"single cheapest decisive candidate\". Also owner-gated: it\nneeds an explicit `Nested(...)` spelling the skill forbids without sign-off. It needed neither the\nedit nor the sign-off.\n\nIts hypothesis is that the `Nested` box exists only because the park arm stores the incoming union.\nThe collapsed allocation view, which the harness could not produce until this week, says **all 3,790\n`Nested` samples on the row, 100%, come from one stack**: `loop$9` → `ProtoKernelBench$.boxed` →\n`Nested.nest` → `Nested$.apply`. That is the *benchmark's own* boxing at the lift boundary. Zero\nsamples reach any park arm, so the eight edits C1 proposes would remove nothing on this row.\n\nLimits stated: one row only (C1 also names the boxing rows, unprofiled), and the inlining confound\napplies as always, though a four-deep stack landing in the benchmark's own `boxed` is not a placement\na park arm could be mistaken for. See `bench-results/c1/RESULT.md`.\n\nIt forced one tool fix: the first attribution named `Nested$.apply`, a type's own factory, which is\nwhere every instance of it is allocated and decides nothing. The report now names the first frame\noutside the allocated type's own code as well. **266 checks green.**\n\n## Three more candidates read from evidence already on disk\n\nNo run spent. See `bench-results/premises/RESULT.md`.\n\n- **IN-1's stated field is dead.** `Arrow$Identity$::apply` is 92 B and *inlined at all 25 sites*, so\n  there is no refusal for a fast/slow split to flip and the candidate's own falsifier is satisfied\n  before the edit is written. Not a refutation of the candidate, a refutation of the field it chose:\n  the effect worth looking for is whether freeing 86 B in 25 callers lets something else in.\n- **IN-3's headline number is not checkable against this instrument.** It claims one\n  `AtomicReferenceArray.get` force-inlines 434 B; the log reports that callee at 12 B. Both can be\n  true, since 434 is the transitive VarHandle expansion the log does not show. Its second field,\n  `javap` of the hot unit, is the right one. Also owner-gated.\n- **IN-2's premise holds and its targets are ranked.** `Stack::truncate` is 52 B against the 35 B cold\n  budget refused at 2/4 sites, `Stack::grow` 55 B refused at 4/4. One correction: the candidate names\n  `Eval.dump`, which is not in the ranking at all, and omits `Stack::grow`, which is the worse of the\n  two by ratio.\n\nAnd the finding that belongs to no candidate: the method ranked **first**, above every kernel method,\nis `ProtoKernelBench::run$56` at 379 B refused 10/10. It is the benchmark's own closure, the same\nfamily the FreqInlineSize flag moved for a 17.4% score change that had nothing to do with the kernel.\nTwo independent readings now say a material share of these rows is the benchmark's own generated code.\n\n## C4 is FIXED, and the harness caught me contaminating its own measurement\n\nOwner opened an explicit exception to the tooling focus to fix this kernel bug and watch the tooling\nbeing used on it.\n\n**Reproduced, then fixed, 128 tests green.** Red first for the right reason: 50 throws escaping a root\n`eval` lost exactly 50 of 512 depth, one per throw, permanently, on a slot that is per thread. After\nthe fix the same test reports `lost 0`.\n\nThe fix is one `try`/`finally` at `Eval.apply`, matching what `Eval.partial` already carries. The\nreasoning that makes it sufficient, which took two wrong turns to reach:\n\n- `Safepoint.exit` is unprotected in all eight delivery arms **by design**, and does not need\n  protecting. Every normal path balances its pairs, *including a drained budget*: the arm that parks\n  never completed an `enter`, and every frame that did runs its `exit` as the parked value propagates\n  up. So only an exception can skip an `exit`.\n- All eight catch sites in `Eval.scala` rethrow, so no exception is absorbed mid-drive and every one\n  reaches a boundary. There are exactly two boundaries and only one was guarded. **That asymmetry was\n  the entire bug.**\n- `save` not `peek`, so a nested eval gets its own budget rather than inheriting a drained one.\n\nTwo wrong turns, both recorded in `bench-results/c4/RESULT.md` because both were plausible: `peek`\ninstead of `save`, and a reset on every trampoline iteration (an unconditional write on the kernel's\nhottest loop, correcting a drift that cannot happen).\n\n**The tooling finding, which is the point of the exercise.** The first bracket failed with\n`⛔ leg control-2 sources changed mid-run`. That is the harness's own guard, firing correctly, because\nI was editing kernel sources in the throwaway worktree while a measurement was in flight. It refused\nto produce a number from a tree that changed underneath it, which is exactly the corruption it exists\nto prevent, and it caught the operator rather than a hypothetical one. Re-run in flight against the\ncommitted fix (`9685c9b445` against `2fc76b9cc6`), store `bench-results/c4-store2`.\n\nThe other half of the finding stands from before: **the harness has no path for a candidate whose\ndeliverable is a failing test.** The diagnosis and the fix came from reading and from sbt; the tool\ncontributed the guard above and will contribute the cost measurement, and nothing else.\n\n### How C4 was diagnosed, before the reproduction existed\n\nSuperseded by the section above, which carries the outcome. Kept for the reasoning, and read as\nhistory rather than as state.\n\nThe only candidate whose deliverable is a failing test, in the list to see whether the harness can\nhandle one. It cannot: every shape it models ends in a Run, a Comparison and a Verdict over benchmark\nrows, and a failing test produces none of those. The *symptom* is measurable though, since a leaked\ndepth forces parks and parks allocate, so `gc.alloc.rate.norm` could carry the confirmation even\nthough nothing in the harness carries the diagnosis.\n\nThe candidate says `Safepoint.exit` is unguarded at the eight delivery arms. It is, and that is by\ndesign, confirmed by the owner: a `try`/`finally` at each would put an exception handler on the\nhottest path in the kernel. The design puts one guard at the boundary instead, and `Eval.partial` has\nit: `save` / `arm` / `try` / `finally restore`.\n\nThe hole is that the **root** entry does not:\n\n    def apply[A](v: A < Any): A =\n        Nested.unnest[A](loop(v, armed = false, neverStop))\n\nEvery top-level `.eval` goes through that. A throw escaping it unwinds past every skipped\n`Safepoint.exit` with nothing restoring the depth, and the slot is per thread, so the loss is paid by\nlater unrelated computations on that thread. No wrong answers, just a thread that parks more and\nallocates more forever after, which is how this stays hidden.\n\n**Diagnosed by reading, so it is a hypothesis until the reproduction fails for the right reason.**\nSee `bench-results/c4/RESULT.md`.\n\n## IN-2 refuted, and more strongly than its own analysis claimed\n\nNo run spent; both readings came from evidence already stored. See `bench-results/in2/RESULT.md`.\n\nIN-2 predicted it would change no score, and that prediction is right. Its reasoning is not, on three\ncounts. **`Eval.dump` has nothing to fix**: 92 B, inlined at both sites, so its falsifier is satisfied\nbefore any edit. **\"Both already inline hot\" is wrong for the other target**: `Stack::truncate` is\nrefused at 2 of 4 sites for size. **The method with the strongest refusal is not in the candidate at\nall**: `Stack::grow`, 55 B, refused 4 of 4.\n\nThen the CPU profile settles it in one line: **no `Stack` or `dump` frame is sampled at all**, in 28\nframes. A refusal costs only when the call happens, so a method the profile never reaches cannot be\nworth an inlining verdict however far over budget it sits. The JIT says the same from its side, having\nrefused the 7-byte `Stack::apply` at 4 of 5 sites for *low call site frequency* rather than for size.\n\nLimits stated: one row profiled, the log carries no invocation counts for these callees, and a\n28-frame profile is directional only.\n\n**Third independent reading of the same underlying finding**: 29.1% of this row is `boxToInteger` and\nthe next three frames, 41.4% more, are the benchmark's own generated methods. 70% of the profile is\ncode no kernel change touches.\n\n## Phase 7 is done, and the dead code was hiding a real one\n\n`MinCpuSamples` was declared and never read. `NoiseShare` was a case class nothing ever constructed.\n`bench-harness-qa.md` was already gone.\n\nThe third item was not dead code but a **duplicate**: `bracketPlan` builds the C V C V C ordering and\n`bracket` built the same ordering again inline, so the test pinning the ordering covered a function\nthe runner did not call, and the ordering that actually ran was pinned by nothing. `bracketPlan` is\nnow generic in what a leg measures and both call it.\n\nThe README drift was real too: it described the throwaway-worktree guard as comparing git dirs, which\nis what the code did before it was changed to require a detached HEAD, and the reason for that change\n(a git-dir comparison catches only the *primary* worktree, while the tree that must not be scribbled\non is whichever one work happens in) had not reached the document. Corrected, along with the four\ncommands the README never listed and the four newer refusals.\n\n## Phase 6 Tier B is done: a pair is now told what it cannot say\n\nA bracket measures the difference between two trees. Attributing that difference to one change inside\nit requires the partition to have been declared, and a pair does not declare one. Every two-sha\ncomparison now says so in the report: the diff may contain any number of changes, so a sentence of the\nform \"this moved because of change X\" is not supported by anything in it, however plausible X is.\n\nA configuration comparison, the same sha under two sets of JVM args, has nothing to partition and gets\nno note. A step of a declared chain gets the opposite note, that its delta *is* isolated.\n\n`bench chain` runs three or more shas, legs interleaved across shas rather than grouped so machine\ndrift does not land entirely in one step, and renders each adjacent pair as its own replicated\ncomparison. It refuses a pair, and refuses a repeated sha, before the worktree is touched at all:\nverified against a nonexistent worktree path, which it never looked at.\n\nThis is the skill's own worked example made mechanical. A node-layout change and a currency hoist\nshipped together, the bundle was faster, the win was credited first to one and then to the other, and\nboth stories were wrong as told. **284 checks green.**\n\n## Defect 9's mitigation is wired in: a dirty A/A null now stops the session\n\nThe null already ran on every bracket, so \"runs on request\" was not the gap. The gap was that its\nfailure was a printed line with a cross on it, and the process exited 0. Every row an A/A null\nclassifies is a false positive by construction, so a dirty null is the strongest available statement\nthat the session is unreadable, and it was the one statement the tool made in passing.\n\nIt is now a blocker, in the same banner and behind the same exit code as an unsettled leg, naming the\nrows it falsely classified. A session with too few control legs to run a null at all is blocked too,\nfor a stronger reason: it cannot check itself. **274 checks green.**\n\n## Validation against the manual work: COMPLETE\n\nThree-way comparison of raw data, tool verdict, and recorded claim, per experiment. The raw data was\nthe arbiter; two of three agreeing settled nothing.\n\n| exp | ingested | tool verdict | 3-way table | disagreements discharged |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| exp3 sweep | yes | yes | yes | yes, 3 of 3 |\n| exp1 budget probes | yes | yes | yes | yes |\n| exp2 forced inline | yes | yes | yes | yes |\n| exp4 escape analysis | yes | yes | yes | yes |\n| exp5 tier splits | yes | yes | yes | yes |\n\n**Stream complete.** See `VALIDATION.md`. Every numeric claim survived; several confidences did not.\nThree of five comparisons are now blocked on a control leg that never settled, and the sweep's fifth\n\"win\" was never a win.\n\n### Findings from this stream, all discharged\n\n1. **`Bench.compare` had no floor at the legs' own error.** Classified -9.8% a win on a row whose\n   control leg reports ±15.2%. *Tool wrong.* **Fixed**: single-pair comparison floors at the legs'\n   own error and states that a floor is not a replicate-estimated threshold.\n2. **No steady-state detection from the iteration series.** *Tool could not express it.* **Fixed**:\n   `unsettledStart` judges by how far the first iteration drags the mean the verdict uses. Two\n   earlier criteria were tried against real data and failed: a fixed percentage cannot work, and an\n   outlier test cannot either, since two real rows trip it at 2.43x and 2.53x with only one a genuine\n   ramp. Both rows are pinned as fixtures.\n3. **`TOOL-VERDICT.md` claimed \"the tool is right each time\".** *False.* **Corrected**, error left\n   visible.\n\n### And the change that came out of it\n\nAn unsettled leg is now a **blocker**, not a warning: banner rendered first, data still printed in\nfull, process exits non-zero. A warning line in a thirty-line report is something this operator\ndemonstrably skips. On the real sweep it fires once, on the true positive, and exits 1.\n\n## Done\n\n- Plan through three review rounds; v4 is current.\n- Phase 1 instruments, Phase 3 A/A null and bracket orchestration, Phase 4 bytecode, Phase 8\n  known-answer fixture, the verdict statistic, efficacy gate, budget-proximity ranking, JVM args per\n  leg, drift off the session path, the ingest path.\n- All 12 implementation-review findings closed.\n- Phase 5 (allocation attribution), Phase 6 Tier A (the investigator), the CLI QA, and the\n  never-exercised guards. **324 checks green across eight suites** is the current figure; the counts\n  quoted inside the sections above are the counts as of those steps and are left as written.\n- Experiment data force-added to git; `.gitignore` had a global `*.json` hiding all of it.\n\n## How defect 8 was closed, and the wrong first version of the fix\n\n`BenchPlan` forecasts each row's detectable effect before a session is spent. Three runs were spent\nreporting a 25% timing regression on a row that resolves to ±22.6% and cannot support a verdict of\nthat size, and each was believed at the time.\n\nIts first version was wrong in the way this campaign keeps being wrong: it estimated between-leg\nspread from a single leg's *within-leg* error, which the fork calibration had already shown are\ndifferent quantities. It called `continuationBodiesFuse` unresolvable at ±14.6% when a real bracket\nresolved a -6.8% win on it, and would have talked me out of the campaign's best measurement.\n\nCorrected to use between-leg spread when legs exist, and to label the single-leg case an\napproximation. Validated against the bracket that refuted it: forecast ±1.5% for\n`continuationBodiesFuse` (bracket resolved -6.8%) and ±15.0% for `trailingMapsStayLinear` (bracket\nreported ±22.6%, called +9.5% flat). Same conclusions, both rows.\n\n## Open, beyond the validation stream\n\n- **Phase 6 Tier B**: a bracket that accepts a *chain* of shas, so a source-level mechanism can be\n  isolated. With two shas the harness must refuse any source-level claim and say the partition was\n  never declared. Tier A (the falsifiers that are JVM flags) is done.\n- **Phase 7 remainder**: dead code (`MinCpuSamples`, `NoiseShare`, stranded doc comments, README\n  drift) and deleting `bench-harness-qa.md`. The guards it named are all exercised now.\n- **DIS-1 is closed: refuted in all three constructible forms.** See above. The remaining candidates\n  in `optimization-plan.md` are untouched.\n- **The sweep was never replicated**: one leg per configuration.\n- **Twenty-three tool defects** in `tool-defects.md`: twenty-one fixed, one bounded, one open, one an observation.\n\n## The kernel result, for a reader arriving cold\n\n`continuationBodiesFuse` was slower under the current design than the old one and nobody knew why.\nThe cause is `kyo.kernel.proto.Eval$::dispatch$1`, 607 bytes, refused by HotSpot as `hot method too\nbig` and present only in the current design: `ask.map{...}` used to mint a `Suspend`, expanded into\nthe drive loop, and now mints a `SuspendWith` whose delivery is that separate method.\n\nForcing it inline takes the row from +4.5% to -6.9%, with the efficacy gate proving the flag took\n(0 inlined / 2 refused becomes 2 inlined / 0 refused). Across all fifteen rows that crude fix wins on\nfour and costs `trailingMapsStayLinear` 23.8% and 239,976 B/op, which a further isolation showed is\nexactly the scalar replacement the enlarged compilation unit destroys: disabling escape analysis on\nthe unmodified design reproduces the same allocation to within 24 bytes of 2.5 million.\n\nTwo tier-split variants aimed at capturing the win without that cost both regress the handler rows by\n22 to 35%. A third variant, which finds the stack index once so a fast-path miss does not pay for a\nsecond scan, is written and compiles with 126 tests green but **has never been measured**.\n\n## The one tool defect still open\n\n**9, synthetic validation agrees with the code's blind spots.** Not fully fixable: every fixture is\nwritten by the same understanding that wrote the code. The mitigation is the A/A null, whose input is\nnot authored, and it has earned that keep twice: catching a missing floor that 31 unit tests and a\nsimulation-backed review missed, and catching a forecast that would have talked me out of the\ncampaign's best measurement. **It still runs on request rather than on every session, and that is the\nopen part.**\n\n### Closed, kept for the reasoning (defects 6 and 8)\n\n**8, resolution reported only after spending the session.** *Fixed by `BenchPlan`.* A five-leg session at one fork resolves\nto ±5.77%, so it cannot see the +4.5% regression this campaign is about, and that was discovered by\nrunning it and reading the footer. Everything needed to say so first is already stored: any prior run\non the same rows carries each leg's `scoreError`. A `bench plan` subcommand should take the intended\nconfiguration and a target effect size, and answer whether the configuration can resolve it, refusing\nor warning when it cannot. Calibration measured earlier says forks will not help, since the variance\nis between legs rather than within them, so the answer will usually be \"more legs\" and it should say\nthat rather than leaving the operator to guess.\n\n**6, a malformed JVM flag produces a normal-looking run.** *Fixed: a rejected compile command fails\nthe leg.* Two runs were spent before a log line\nrevealed `CompileCommand: An error occurred during parsing`. The harness must assert that a compile\ncommand it issued was parsed, and prefer the file form, which does not have to survive shell and sbt\nquoting. Without this, Phase 6's Tier A would silently test nothing while reporting refutations.\n\n## Standing constraints\n\nNo kernel source landed. {"parentUuid":"a9bce388-08a5-4cce-b0df-4f10b37e875b","isSidechain":true,"promptId":"e8d5459a-a357-48d8-90fc-44d59227e184","agentId":"af5a83bcca1649bc3","type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01MUP6ku1bKF2Kij8PnUoicB","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Where the tool left me guessing\n2\t\n3\tRecorded while running Experiment 1, which is the point of QA-ing the harness by using it. Two\n4\tthings were under test: the candidate, and the tool. The tool is the one that matters, and every\n5\tmoment I reached past it for a shell script or a python one-liner is a defect in it.\n6\t\n7\tThe experiment succeeded. The tool contributed almost nothing to that success, which is the finding.\n8\t\n9\t## What I had to do by hand\n10\t\n11\t**1. Run the experiment at all.** The harness has no flag-probe path. I wrote a 25-line shell script\n12\tto restore two designs, issue four JMH invocations with `-jvmArgsAppend`, and collect the json.\n13\t`runLeg` cannot take extra JVM arguments, so even with the harness running I could not have asked it\n14\tfor this. *This is Phase 6 Tier A, unimplemented: the entire point of that phase is that a falsifier\n15\twhich is a JVM flag can be derived from the hypothesis and run automatically.*\n16\t\n17\t**2. The efficacy gate.** The protocol demands proving a flag took effect before reading its result.\n18\tThe tool has no function for it. I wrote 40 lines of python to parse two compilation logs, group C2\n19\tinline verdicts by method, and diff them. `LogCompilation` already produces exactly this structure;\n20\twhat is missing is a `diff(a, b)` over two `Parsed` values. Without that, the most important guard in\n21\tthe protocol is a manual step, which means in practice it is an optional one.\n22\t\n23\t**3. Finding the 379-byte method.** The mechanism was `run$56` at 379 bytes refused for\n24\t`hot method too big`. The tool holds every part of that (per-site verdicts, byte sizes, reasons) and\n25\twould not have surfaced it, because nothing ranks refusals by whether they sit near a budget\n26\tthreshold. `Bytecode.Change.crossedBudget` does exactly this reasoning for a size *change* between\n27\tlegs; the same question about an absolute size against the budget is not asked anywhere.\n28\t\n29\t**4. Comparing two configurations of one design.** Every comparison the harness models is\n30\tdesign-against-design. Configuration-against-configuration, the same sources under two JVM settings,\n31\thas no representation at all, though it is the shape of every Tier A falsifier.\n32\t\n33\t**5. Replication.** I ran one configuration per cell. The harness's own statistic needs C V C V C and\n34\tits runner still produces one leg per invocation, so the thresholds and the minimum detectable effect\n35\tI built tonight could not be applied to the one measurement that was actually taken. The numbers are\n36\treported as approximate for exactly this reason.\n37\t\n38\t## What the tool did contribute\n39\t\n40\tThe discipline, which is not nothing. Heap and collector pinned because the plan says to. The\n41\tefficacy gate run *before* the numbers were read, because the protocol says to, and it is the step\n42\tthat turned a suggestive result into a named mechanism. The reading rules written down in advance,\n43\tso the interpretation was fixed before the data existed. And the honest limits section, which exists\n44\tbecause the plan requires every result to state what it does not establish.\n45\t\n46\tThat is the harness working as a procedure while contributing nothing as a program.\n47\t\n48\t## Ranked fixes\n49\t\n50\t1. **`LogCompilation.diff`** over two `Parsed` values, returning per-method verdict changes. Turns the\n51\t   efficacy gate from 40 lines of throwaway python into a call. Cheapest and highest value.\n52\t2. **`runLeg` accepting extra JVM arguments**, and a configuration-pair comparison alongside the\n53\t   design-pair one. Without these Tier A cannot exist.\n54\t3. **Rank refusals by proximity to a budget.** A method refused `hot method too big` at 379 bytes\n55\t   against a 325 default is a finding; the same refusal at 4000 bytes is furniture.\n56\t4. **Leg orchestration for C V C V C**, so the statistic that is implemented and tested can actually\n57\t   be applied to a measurement.\n58\t\n59\tNothing here is a surprise: items 1, 2 and 4 are Phases 6 and 3 of the plan, unimplemented. The value\n60\tof running the experiment first is knowing which order to build them in, and that item 3 was not in\n61\tthe plan at all.\n62\t\n63\t## Added after experiment 2\n64\t\n65\t**6. A malformed JVM flag produces a completely normal-looking run.** `-XX:CompileCommand=inline,...`\n66\ton a Scala method name cannot survive the shell and sbt quoting chain: two runs were spent before the\n67\tlog showed `CompileCommand: An error occurred during parsing`, and both had produced plausible\n68\toutput. `CompileCommandFile` avoids the escaping entirely. The harness must, when it issues a compile\n69\tcommand, assert that the JVM parsed it, and must prefer the file form. Without that, Phase 6 Tier A\n70\twould silently test nothing while reporting refutations.\n71\t\n72\t**7. The efficacy gate earned its place twice, in opposite directions.** On the budget probes it\n73\tshowed the flag never achieved the intended state (`dispatch$1` refused at 600 and at 700, for two\n74\tdifferent reasons), which made those runs inconclusive rather than evidence against the hypothesis.\n75\tOn the forced-inline run it showed the change took exactly, which is what licensed reading the score.\n76\tA harness without it would have concluded the opposite of the truth from the same four numbers.\n77\t\n78\t## Added after the first real bracket\n79\t\n80\t**8. The harness reports its resolution only after spending the session.** The A/A at five legs and\n81\tone fork resolves to ±5.77%, which means it cannot see the +4.55% regression this campaign was built\n82\taround. That was discovered by running the session and reading the footer. A tool whose purpose is to\n83\tprevent wasted conclusions should say, before the first leg, what effect size the requested\n84\tconfiguration can detect, and refuse or warn when the target effect is below it. Everything needed is\n85\talready there: the legs' own errors are in the JMH json of any prior run on the same rows.\n86\t\n87\t**9. Synthetic validation agrees with the code's blind spots by construction.** The replicate\n88\tstatistic had 31 unit tests, a simulation-backed review, and three rounds of plan review, and none of\n89\tthem found a missing `max` between the threshold and the legs' own error. Five legs of identical\n90\tsources on a real machine found it in one run. Every fixture in this suite was generated by the same\n91\tunderstanding that wrote the code under it; the A/A is the only check whose input the author does not\n92\tcontrol. It should run on every session, not on request.\n93\t\n94\t\n95\t## Added by the first QA of the CLI surface\n96\t\n97\tEvery defect above was found by using the tool on kernel questions. Nobody had ever run its\n98\tcommands *wrong* on purpose, which is the other half of what a tool has to survive. Four of the six\n99\tsubcommands were exercised with a typo, a missing file, and a mismatched argument count.\n100\t\n101\t**14, a store that does not exist reads as a store that is empty.** `bench list --store <typo>`\n102\tprinted `no runs stored` and exited 0. So a mistyped path, a store on a different branch, and a store\n103\twhose runs really were deleted are three different situations the tool reported identically, and the\n104\tone that is an operator error is the one it is silent about. This is the campaign's own failure shape\n105\tarriving through the front door: a clean-looking result standing in for an unasked question.\n106\t**Fixed**: reading a store requires it to exist. `bench list`, `show`, `compare` and `plan` fail with\n107\tthe path and what would have created it.\n108\t\n109\t**15, an unknown run id was answered with a file path and a stack trace.**\n110\t`bench show --id nope` produced `Failure(kyo.FileNotFoundException: ... /runs/nope.json ...)` and then\n111\tthe same text again under `Exception in thread \"main\"`. Two renders of one problem, both naming a\n112\tpath the operator never typed, neither naming the ids that do exist. **Fixed**: the failure names the\n113\tid, lists what the store holds, and prints once. The doubling is upstream: `KyoAppRunner.onResult`\n114\tprints the result and then rethrows any `Throwable` error, so every kyo app that fails through\n115\t`Abort` renders its failure twice. The harness now catches its own failures before they reach that\n116\tpath; the observation about kyo stands separately.\n117\t\n118\t**16, a leftover argument was dropped without a word.** `bench ingest` with two json files and three\n119\tshas used the first two and discarded the third, so a mis-typed invocation ingested under shas the\n120\toperator did not intend. **Fixed**: the count must be one per file or one for all.\n121\t\n122\t## Added by using the investigator on the campaign's own data\n123\t\n124\t**17, adding a field to `Run` made every stored run undecodable.** All 34, across six stores, with the\n125\tcampaign's whole measurement history behind them. The tool reported it clearly and refused, which is\n126\tcorrect, but the store is the durable record and a schema addition must leave the old records\n127\treadable. **Fixed**: the field is defaulted, and a test decodes a run recorded before it existed.\n128\t\n129\t**18, the escape-analysis falsifier was adjudicated on wall clock.** It is a claim about bytes per\n130\toperation, and the row it fires on is one whose *timing does not resolve at all*, so judging it on\n131\ttiming answers a question nobody asked. Found by running the new rule table against the real sweep.\n132\t**Fixed**: each hypothesis names the quantity that answers it.\n133\t\n134\t**19, a one-byte allocation band refused the campaign's own result.** `gc.alloc.rate.norm` is nearly\n135\texact, and \"nearly\" had been assumed rather than measured: the escape-analysis isolation landed 23.8 B\n136\tfrom its target on 2.56 MB, a reproduction to six significant figures, and was reported inconclusive.\n137\t**Fixed**, from data: across four A/A sets of three legs on identical sources, every kilobyte-scale\n138\trow reproduced to the byte and the one megabyte-scale row spread 47.8 B on 2.32 MB. The band is 5e-5\n139\trelative with a one-byte floor, twice the worst observed spread, and 1,875x smaller than the effect it\n140\thas to resolve.\n141\t\n142\t## Added by exercising the guards that had never fired\n143\t\n144\t**20, a leg could adopt the previous leg's numbers.** The results json is a fixed path per label and\n145\twas never deleted before a run. JMH exits 0 when its selector matches nothing, which is the exact\n146\tfailure the retry beside it exists for, so such a run would leave the previous attempt's file in place\n147\tand this leg would parse it, pass the row-count check, and be stored as a measurement of sources it\n148\tnever ran against. **Fixed**: the file is deleted before every attempt, and its absence afterwards\n149\tfails the leg with the reason.\n150\t\n151\t**21, the red-tree gate had never refused anything.** Verified for the first time by planting a\n152\tfailing test in the throwaway worktree: `sbt --client` does exit 1 on a test failure, `exec` does\n153\tabort, and the leg does not run. The gate works. What did not was its message: `Failure(1)` followed\n154\tby several hundred lines of *passing* test names, with the one line naming the failure far below the\n155\tfold. **Fixed**: a failed command reports its error lines and its tail, and says how much it left out.\n156\t\n157\t**22, a QA check that passed whenever nothing was flagged.** `QaEndToEnd`'s steady-state check read\n158\t`stillCompiling(ctl).isEmpty || out.contains(\"NOT STEADY STATE\")`, so on every run ever made it\n159\tasserted nothing. **Fixed** to the biconditional it meant.\n160\t\n161\t**23, the steady-state compile-time limit cannot be calibrated from any data this campaign has.** It\n162\twas 1.0% of the measured window, 50 ms, against an observed maximum of 9 ms across 52 stored rows, so\n163\tit has never fired and could not have. The plan called for tightening it to the ~4 ms of the run that\n164\tmotivated it; that would be wrong, because 8 of those 52 rows sit at or above 4 ms and every one is\n165\tordinary. Nor is there a positive case to fit: of the 25 rows carrying both an iteration series and a\n166\tcompile-time figure, none is unsettled by the series criterion. **Bounded rather than fixed**: set to\n167\t0.5%, under three times the worst share observed, and documented as not-yet-validated. The signal\n168\tactually catching unsettled legs is `Row.unsettledStart`.\n169\t\n170\t## Defect 9's mitigation, wired in\n171\t\n172\t**24, a dirty A/A null printed a line and exited 0.** The null runs on every bracket, so the \"runs on\n173\trequest\" half of defect 9 was already closed; what was not is that its failure was reported as a\n174\twarning. Every row an A/A null classifies is a false positive by construction, comparing control legs\n175\tagainst each other, so a dirty null is the strongest statement available that the session below is\n176\tunreadable, and it was the one statement the tool made in passing. **Fixed**: it is a blocker, in the\n177\tsame banner and behind the same exit code as an unsettled leg, naming the rows it falsely classified.\n178\t\n179\tA session with too few control legs is blocked too, and for a stronger reason: it is not that the\n180\tcheck failed, it is that the session cannot check itself. That also used to be a printed line.\n181\t\n182\t## Found by reading a real verdict\n183\t\n184\t**26, two fixed decimals made a nanosecond row unreadable.** The C4 bracket regressed\n185\t`evalFixedOverhead` by 26.2%, cleanly separated and not marginal, and the report rendered it as\n186\t`0.01 ± 0.00` against `0.01 ± 0.00`. The numbers behind the verdict were invisible and the error\n187\tcolumn read as though there were no error at all; the real values were 0.005853 ± 0.000317 against\n188\t0.007364 ± 0.000111, which any reader could have judged on sight.\n189\t\n190\tThe skill requires that a reader judge a result without asking what was measured or how confident it\n191\tis, and requires the error column specifically because a delta smaller than the combined error is not\n192\ta result. Rounding both to zero defeats both rules at once. **Fixed**: precision scales with\n193\tmagnitude, and the same stored runs re-read correctly with no re-run, since a comparison is a pure\n194\tfunction over records.\n195\t\n196\t## Found by trying to replicate the sweep\n197\t\n198\t**25, a stored run did not record the JVM arguments that produced it.** A configuration comparison\n199\tvaries nothing but those arguments, so a stored pair with the same `sha` and the same `treeHash` is\n200\totherwise indistinguishable. The campaign's **headline result** is stored exactly that way:\n201\t`continuationBodiesFuse` at -6.8% under a forced inline, with the forcing recorded nowhere. Those runs\n202\tcan be loaded, re-compared and re-reported forever, and no reader can say what was measured. The\n203\tcompile-command file that produced them is no longer on disk either, so the configuration is\n204\tunrecoverable rather than merely unstated.\n205\t\n206\tThis is the same family as defect 11: the harness gained the ability to *express* configuration\n207\tcomparisons (`Arm(sha, jvmArgs)`) without gaining the ability to *record* one.\n208\t\n209\t**Fixed**: `Run.jvmArgs`, defaulted so the 34 stored runs still decode, and a same-sha comparison now\n210\tprints exactly which arguments differ. Measured against the replicated sweep, forecast against actual:\n234\t\n235\t| row | forecast | actual | |\n236\t|---|---|---|---|\n237\t| `handleLoopAnswersInPlace` | ±10.0% | ±14.4% | under by 1.4x |\n238\t| `continuationBodiesFuse` | ±1.9% | ±3.6% | under by 1.9x |\n239\t| `suspensionBaseline` | ±3.2% | ±3.9% | under |\n240\t| `handleLoopFusesContinuation` | ±6.8% | ±5.8% | over |\n241\t| `emittingClausesPayRegionRebuild` | ±14.6% | ±12.6% | over |\n242\t\n243\t**Fixed, and the diagnosis had three parts, the third found by the test rather than by me.** It lumped every prior leg into one spread, which sees only\n244\tone arm's variance when given one arm and folds the real between-arm difference into the \"spread\" when\n245\tgiven both. And it normalised against the mean of *every* leg\n248\twhere the threshold divides by the **control** mean, which understates the forecast whenever the arms\n249\tgenuinely differ: on `trailingMapsStayLinear`, whose variant runs a third slower than its control,\n250\tthat alone put the forecast 8.8 points below the threshold it was predicting.\n251\t\n252\tWith all three corrections, forecasting the replicated sweep from its own legs reproduces **all 15**\n253\tof the thresholds that bracket produced, most of them to a tenth of a point, including\n254\t`trailingMapsStayLinear` at ±59.9% against ±59.9%. `PlanTest` pins that as a relationship rather than\n255\ta table of constants, so it fails if either estimator drifts.\n256\t\n257\t**A claim of mine that the test refuted.** I recorded that a one-arm forecast is \"systematically\n258\toptimistic\". Two\nthings were under test: the candidate, and the tool. The tool is the one that matters, and every\nmoment I reached past it for a shell script or a python one-liner is a defect in it.\n\nThe experiment succeeded. The tool contributed almost nothing to that success, which is the finding.\n\n## What I had to do by hand\n\n**1. Run the experiment at all.** The harness has no flag-probe path. I wrote a 25-line shell script\nto restore two designs, issue four JMH invocations with `-jvmArgsAppend`, and collect the json.\n`runLeg` cannot take extra JVM arguments, so even with the harness running I could not have asked it\nfor this. *This is Phase 6 Tier A, unimplemented: the entire point of that phase is that a falsifier\nwhich is a JVM flag can be derived from the hypothesis and run automatically.*\n\n**2. The efficacy gate.** The protocol demands proving a flag took effect before reading its result.\nThe tool has no function for it. I wrote 40 lines of python to parse two compilation logs, group C2\ninline verdicts by method, and diff them. `LogCompilation` already produces exactly this structure;\nwhat is missing is a `diff(a, b)` over two `Parsed` values. Without that, the most important guard in\nthe protocol is a manual step, which means in practice it is an optional one.\n\n**3. Finding the 379-byte method.** The mechanism was `run$56` at 379 bytes refused for\n`hot method too big`. The tool holds every part of that (per-site verdicts, byte sizes, reasons) and\nwould not have surfaced it, because nothing ranks refusals by whether they sit near a budget\nthreshold. `Bytecode.Change.crossedBudget` does exactly this reasoning for a size *change* between\nlegs; the same question about an absolute size against the budget is not asked anywhere.\n\n**4. Comparing two configurations of one design.** Every comparison the harness models is\ndesign-against-design. Configuration-against-configuration, the same sources under two JVM settings,\nhas no representation at all, though it is the shape of every Tier A falsifier.\n\n**5. Replication.** I ran one configuration per cell. The harness's own statistic needs C V C V C and\nits runner still produces one leg per invocation, so the thresholds and the minimum detectable effect\nI built tonight could not be applied to the one measurement that was actually taken. The numbers are\nreported as approximate for exactly this reason.\n\n## What the tool did contribute\n\nThe discipline, which is not nothing. Heap and collector pinned because the plan says to. The\nefficacy gate run *before* the numbers were read, because the protocol says to, and it is the step\nthat turned a suggestive result into a named mechanism. The reading rules written down in advance,\nso the interpretation was fixed before the data existed. And the honest limits section, which exists\nbecause the plan requires every result to state what it does not establish.\n\nThat is the harness working as a procedure while contributing nothing as a program.\n\n## Ranked fixes\n\n1. **`LogCompilation.diff`** over two `Parsed` values, returning per-method verdict changes. Turns the\n   efficacy gate from 40 lines of throwaway python into a call. Cheapest and highest value.\n2. **`runLeg` accepting extra JVM arguments**, and a configuration-pair comparison alongside the\n   design-pair one. Without these Tier A cannot exist.\n3. **Rank refusals by proximity to a budget.** A method refused `hot method too big` at 379 bytes\n   against a 325 default is a finding; the same refusal at 4000 bytes is furniture.\n4. **Leg orchestration for C V C V C**, so the statistic that is implemented and tested can actually\n   be applied to a measurement.\n\nNothing here is a surprise: items 1, 2 and 4 are Phases 6 and 3 of the plan, unimplemented. The value\nof running the experiment first is knowing which order to build them in, and that item 3 was not in\nthe plan at all.\n\n## Added after experiment 2\n\n**6. A malformed JVM flag produces a completely normal-looking run.** `-XX:CompileCommand=inline,...`\non a Scala method name cannot survive the shell and sbt quoting chain: two runs were spent before the\nlog showed `CompileCommand: An error occurred during parsing`, and both had produced plausible\noutput. `CompileCommandFile` avoids the escaping entirely. The harness must, when it issues a compile\ncommand, assert that the JVM parsed it, and must prefer the file form. Without that, Phase 6 Tier A\nwould silently test nothing while reporting refutations.\n\n**7. The efficacy gate earned its place twice, in opposite directions.** On the budget probes it\nshowed the flag never achieved the intended state (`dispatch$1` refused at 600 and at 700, for two\ndifferent reasons), which made those runs inconclusive rather than evidence against the hypothesis.\nOn the forced-inline run it showed the change took exactly, which is what licensed reading the score.\nA harness without it would have concluded the opposite of the truth from the same four numbers.\n\n## Added after the first real bracket\n\n**8. The harness reports its resolution only after spending the session.** The A/A at five legs and\none fork resolves to ±5.77%, which means it cannot see the +4.55% regression this campaign was built\naround. That was discovered by running the session and reading the footer. A tool whose purpose is to\nprevent wasted conclusions should say, before the first leg, what effect size the requested\nconfiguration can detect, and refuse or warn when the target effect is below it. Everything needed is\nalready there: the legs' own errors are in the JMH json of any prior run on the same rows.\n\n**9. Synthetic validation agrees with the code's blind spots by construction.** The replicate\nstatistic had 31 unit tests, a simulation-backed review, and three rounds of plan review, and none of\nthem found a missing `max` between the threshold and the legs' own error. Five legs of identical\nsources on a real machine found it in one run. Every fixture in this suite was generated by the same\nunderstanding that wrote the code under it; the A/A is the only check whose input the author does not\ncontrol. It should run on every session, not on request.\n\n\n## Added by the first QA of the CLI surface\n\nEvery defect above was found by using the tool on kernel questions. Nobody had ever run its\ncommands *wrong* on purpose, which is the other half of what a tool has to survive. Four of the six\nsubcommands were exercised with a typo, a missing file, and a mismatched argument count.\n\n**14, a store that does not exist reads as a store that is empty.** `bench list --store <typo>`\nprinted `no runs stored` and exited 0. So a mistyped path, a store on a different branch, and a store\nwhose runs really were deleted are three different situations the tool reported identically, and the\none that is an operator error is the one it is silent about. This is the campaign's own failure shape\narriving through the front door: a clean-looking result standing in for an unasked question.\n**Fixed**: reading a store requires it to exist. `bench list`, `show`, `compare` and `plan` fail with\nthe path and what would have created it.\n\n**15, an unknown run id was answered with a file path and a stack trace.**\n`bench show --id nope` produced `Failure(kyo.FileNotFoundException: ... /runs/nope.json ...)` and then\nthe same text again under `Exception in thread \"main\"`. Two renders of one problem, both naming a\npath the operator never typed, neither naming the ids that do exist. **Fixed**: the failure names the\nid, lists what the store holds, and prints once. The doubling is upstream: `KyoAppRunner.onResult`\nprints the result and then rethrows any `Throwable` error, so every kyo app that fails through\n`Abort` renders its failure twice. The harness now catches its own failures before they reach that\npath; the observation about kyo stands separately.\n\n**16, a leftover argument was dropped without a word.** `bench ingest` with two json files and three\nshas used the first two and discarded the third, so a mis-typed invocation ingested under shas the\noperator did not intend. **Fixed**: the count must be one per file or one for all.\n\n## Added by using the investigator on the campaign's own data\n\n**17, adding a field to `Run` made every stored run undecodable.** All 34, across six stores, with the\ncampaign's whole measurement history behind them. The tool reported it clearly and refused, which is\ncorrect, but the store is the durable record and a schema addition must leave the old records\nreadable. **Fixed**: the field is defaulted, and a test decodes a run recorded before it existed.\n\n**18, the escape-analysis falsifier was adjudicated on wall clock.** It is a claim about bytes per\noperation, and the row it fires on is one whose *timing does not resolve at all*, so judging it on\ntiming answers a question nobody asked. Found by running the new rule table against the real sweep.\n**Fixed**: each hypothesis names the quantity that answers it.\n\n**19, a one-byte allocation band refused the campaign's own result.** `gc.alloc.rate.norm` is nearly\nexact, and \"nearly\" had been assumed rather than measured: the escape-analysis isolation landed 23.8 B\nfrom its target on 2.56 MB, a reproduction to six significant figures, and was reported inconclusive.\n**Fixed**, from data: across four A/A sets of three legs on identical sources, every kilobyte-scale\nrow reproduced to the byte and the one megabyte-scale row spread 47.8 B on 2.32 MB. The band is 5e-5\nrelative with a one-byte floor, twice the worst observed spread, and 1,875x smaller than the effect it\nhas to resolve.\n\n## Added by exercising the guards that had never fired\n\n**20, a leg could adopt the previous leg's numbers.** The results json is a fixed path per label and\nwas never deleted before a run. JMH exits 0 when its selector matches nothing, which is the exact\nfailure the retry beside it exists for, so such a run would leave the previous attempt's file in place\nand this leg would parse it, pass the row-count check, and be stored as a measurement of sources it\nnever ran against. **Fixed**: the file is deleted before every attempt, and its absence afterwards\nfails the leg with the reason.\n\n**21, the red-tree gate had never refused anything.** Verified for the first time by planting a\nfailing test in the throwaway worktree: `sbt --client` does exit 1 on a test failure, `exec` does\nabort, and the leg does not run. The gate works. What did not was its message: `Failure(1)` followed\nby several hundred lines of *passing* test names, with the one line naming the failure far below the\nfold. **Fixed**: a failed command reports its error lines and its tail, and says how much it left out.\n\n**22, a QA check that passed whenever nothing was flagged.** `QaEndToEnd`'s steady-state check read\n`stillCompiling(ctl).isEmpty || out.contains(\"NOT STEADY STATE\")`, so on every run ever made it\nasserted nothing. **Fixed** to the biconditional it meant.\n\n**23, the steady-state compile-time limit cannot be calibrated from any data this campaign has.** It\nwas 1.0% of the measured window, 50 ms, against an observed maximum of 9 ms across 52 stored rows, so\nit has never fired and could not have. The plan called for tightening it to the ~4 ms of the run that\nmotivated it; that would be wrong, because 8 of those 52 rows sit at or above 4 ms and every one is\nordinary. Nor is there a positive case to fit: of the 25 rows carrying both an iteration series and a\ncompile-time figure, none is unsettled by the series criterion. **Bounded rather than fixed**: set to\n0.5%, under three times the worst share observed, and documented as not-yet-validated. The signal\nactually catching unsettled legs is `Row.unsettledStart`.\n\n## Defect 9's mitigation, wired in\n\n**24, a dirty A/A null printed a line and exited 0.** The null runs on every bracket, so the \"runs on\nrequest\" half of defect 9 was already closed; what was not is that its failure was reported as a\nwarning. Every row an A/A null classifies is a false positive by construction, comparing control legs\nagainst each other, so a dirty null is the strongest statement available that the session below is\nunreadable, and it was the one statement the tool made in passing. **Fixed**: it is a blocker, in the\nsame banner and behind the same exit code as an unsettled leg, naming the rows it falsely classified.\n\nA session with too few control legs is blocked too, and for a stronger reason: it is not that the\ncheck failed, it is that the session cannot check itself. That also used to be a printed line.\n\n## Found by reading a real verdict\n\n**26, two fixed decimals made a nanosecond row unreadable.** The C4 bracket regressed\n`evalFixedOverhead` by 26.2%, cleanly separated and not marginal, and the report rendered it as\n`0.01 ± 0.00` against `0.01 ± 0.00`. The numbers behind the verdict were invisible and the error\ncolumn read as though there were no error at all; the real values were 0.005853 ± 0.000317 against\n0.007364 ± 0.000111, which any reader could have judged on sight.\n\nThe skill requires that a reader judge a result without asking what was measured or how confident it\nis, and requires the error column specifically because a delta smaller than the combined error is not\na result. Rounding both to zero defeats both rules at once. **Fixed**: precision scales with\nmagnitude, and the same stored runs re-read correctly with no re-run, since a comparison is a pure\nfunction over records.\n\n## Found by trying to replicate the sweep\n\n**25, a stored run did not record the JVM arguments that produced it.** A configuration comparison\nvaries nothing but those arguments, so a stored pair with the same `sha` and the same `treeHash` is\notherwise indistinguishable. The campaign's **headline result** is stored exactly that way:\n`continuationBodiesFuse` at -6.8% under a forced inline, with the forcing recorded nowhere. Those runs\ncan be loaded, re-compared and re-reported forever, and no reader can say what was measured. The\ncompile-command file that produced them is no longer on disk either, so the configuration is\nunrecoverable rather than merely unstated.\n\nThis is the same family as defect 11: the harness gained the ability to *express* configuration\ncomparisons (`Arm(sha, jvmArgs)`) without gaining the ability to *record* one.\n\n**Fixed**: `Run.jvmArgs`, defaulted so the 34 stored runs still decode, and a same-sha comparison now\nprints exactly which arguments differ. A same-sha pair with nothing recorded says so, and names the\ntwo readings, rather than presenting itself as a clean comparison.\n\n## Found by validating one part of the tool against another\n\n**27, a bracket's replicated verdict could not be re-read from its own store.** `bench compare` took\nexactly one control id and one variant id, so once a bracket's legs were stored the only statistic\nrecoverable from them was the **single-pair** one, which is the weaker of the two. So the harness's stated\nprinciple, that a comparison is a pure function over records and two run ids always produce the same\nverdict, held for the weaker claim and silently not for the stronger one, and the stronger one existed\nonly in the terminal scrollback of the run that produced it. **Fixed**: `--control` and `--variant`\nrepeat, and more than one leg on either side selects `compareReplicated`. Re-rendering the sweep from\nits store now reproduces the bracket's own three wins exactly.\n\n**28, the report showed only the worst resolution, never each row's own.** The footer says \"flat to\nwithin its own resolution, at worst ±X\", which cannot answer the question a flat row actually raises:\nwas it close to resolving or nowhere near? On the replicated sweep `emittingClausesPayRegionRebuild`\ncame back flat at **-12.5% against its own ±12.6%**, missing by a tenth of a point, and nothing in the\ntable said so. **Fixed**: a `resolves` column per row.\n\n**29, `BenchPlan` did not reproduce the thresholds it forecasts.** It forecasts from control legs\nonly, while the threshold it is predicting pools the spread of *both* arms, so it cannot see the\nvariance the variant legs contribute. Measured against the replicated sweep, forecast against actual:\n\n| row | forecast | actual | |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| `handleLoopAnswersInPlace` | ±10.0% | ±14.4% | under by 1.4x |\n| `continuationBodiesFuse` | ±1.9% | ±3.6% | under by 1.9x |\n| `suspensionBaseline` | ±3.2% | ±3.9% | under |\n| `handleLoopFusesContinuation` | ±6.8% | ±5.8% | over |\n| `emittingClausesPayRegionRebuild` | ±14.6% | ±12.6% | over |\n\n**Fixed, and the diagnosis had three parts, the third found by the test rather than by me.** It lumped every prior leg into one spread, which sees only\none arm's variance when given one arm and folds the real between-arm difference into the \"spread\" when\ngiven both. It now splits by arm and pools *within* each, exactly as `Stats.pooledSd` does. It\nomitted the floor `Stats.threshold` applies at the legs' own reported error, so it predicted\nresolutions the real comparison would never award. And it normalised against the mean of *every* leg\nwhere the threshold divides by the **control** mean, which understates the forecast whenever the arms\ngenuinely differ: on `trailingMapsStayLinear`, whose variant runs a third slower than its control,\nthat alone put the forecast 8.8 points below the threshold it was predicting.\n\nWith all three corrections, forecasting the replicated sweep from its own legs reproduces **all 15**\nof the thresholds that bracket produced, most of them to a tenth of a point, including\n`trailingMapsStayLinear` at ±59.9% against ±59.9%. `PlanTest` pins that as a relationship rather than\na table of constants, so it fails if either estimator drifts.\n\n**A claim of mine that the test refuted.** I recorded that a one-arm forecast is \"systematically\noptimistic\".
